title: The Athletic’s football analytics glossary: explaining xG, PPDA, field tilt and how to use them - The Athletic
text: The Athletic’s football analytics glossary: explaining xG, PPDA, field tilt and how to use them - The Athletic Film Study The Athletic’s football analytics glossary: explaining xG, PPDA, field tilt and how to use them By Mark Carey and Tom Worville July 28, 2021 Updated April 8, 2026 Share article 75 Our use of data and statistics has been ever-growing within the articles that we write at The Athletic , drawing upon different metrics to highlight strengths, weaknesses, or patterns observed in a certain team or player. Some of these analytics metrics will be very familiar to you by now, while others might need a little bit more explanation. Much like the NFL analytics glossary from The Athletic , this is our attempt at explaining some of the most common football metrics and how to use them. So let’s dive in… 1. “Per 90” metrics What it is: This is an important place to start when outlining metrics in football analytics, at a player and a team level. Using raw, total numbers for a metric can be misleading, as it does not account for the minutes played to reach that number. Context is key, and we need to find a fair way to compare performance by looking at those numbers within the context of a full game (per 90 minutes or “per 90”). Advertisement How it can be used: Since the start of the 2019-20 season, Liverpool’s Sadio Mane has scored 29 goals in the Premier League, while Tammy Abraham has only scored 21 for Chelsea. This would initially point to Mane being the more clinical player in front of goal, but the added context is that Mane has played more than 2,000 minutes more than Abraham in this period. When you look at this goal output per 90, we see Abraham actually scores at a higher rate (0.58 goals per 90) than Mane (0.47 goals per 90) — which makes more sense given their different roles across the forward line. A closer look at the top goalscorers from the 2020-21 season is interesting to see on a per 90 basis. Considering only players who have played 900-plus minutes in the Premier League, the player with the highest goal rate was Tottenham Hotspur loanee Gareth Bale . While he may not have accrued as many minutes as some of his peers, Bale’s rate of more than one goal per 90 minutes is an outstanding return for the time he was on the pitch. 2. Expected goals (xG) What it is: A lot of the football world will have at least heard of xG by now. Put simply, xG is a way to measure the likelihood of a shot becoming a goal. Not all shots are equal in their quality — one shot might be a speculative 40-yarder and another might be a two-yard tap-in. Therefore, xG measures the quality of each shot before the player shoots , taking into account many factors, including: The shot angle The distance from goal Whether it was with the head, or with the weaker/stronger foot Whether it was from a cross, through ball, short pass etc Whether there were multiple defenders in the way It is important to note that different data providers have slight differences in the factors they consider to go into their xG model. Nevertheless, the xG value is always presented as a number between zero (no chance of a goal) and one (a certain goal). For example, this shot below taken by Bruno Fernandes vs Southampton had an xG value of 0.3, which means that the shot would be expected to be a goal 3 times out of 10 (or 30 times out of 100), given the situation he found himself in. The xG value is calculated using thousands of previous shots that were similar to that situation, and seeing how many of those were scored as a result. Importantly, the value does not consider the quality of the player shooting, but instead provides a value based on how the “average” player would perform in a similar situation. Therefore, the quality of a player’s shot execution might significantly improve that chance — which we will come onto next. Advertisement How it can be used: The examples above use xG on a single shot to outline the metric itself, but it is often not too insightful to explore xG on a shot-by-shot basis. What we can do is add up a player or team’s xG throughout a game, period, or season to give a clearer idea of how many goals they should have scored, based on the quality of shots they had. Of course, it is more reliable to draw insight from such information when you have a larger sample to work from, across a longer period of time. When we do this, we can use xG to explore whether a certain player or team is under or over-performing in front of goal compared with their expectation. 3. Expected goals on target (xGOT) What it is: Building on xG, we can dig deeper into the likelihood of a shot becoming a goal. Whereas xG provides a value of the shot before the player shoots , expected goals on target (xGOT) provides a modified value of an on-target shot after the player shoots . The value presented is the same — a number between zero (no chance of a goal) and one (a certain goal). But it adds further context by crediting the shots that head towards the top corner vs those that are straight down the middle of the goal. As you would imagine, this xGOT model only calculates a value for shots that are on target, so relies on the player to at least work the keeper to be registered — of course, if the shot is off-target your chance of scoring a goal is zero (barring an unlikely deflection). Let’s take this example below from Harry Kane last season. Before he takes the shot outside the area, his xG is 0.03 — a low-value chance that would be expected to be a goal only three times out of 100. However, the quality of the strike from Kane is outstanding, as it flies into the top corner. Having taken the shot, the xGOT value of this chance now jumps up to 0.54, meaning that the location of that strike would lead to a goal 54 per cent of the time. A high-quality finish indeed. How it can be used: The main thing xGOT provides is a clearer idea of a player’s shot execution. If a player has an xGOT value that is consistently higher than their xG, this tells us that they are shooting at a better rate than the quality of the chances they are getting. It is worth noting that such figures do only include shots that hit the target, which unfortunately excludes blocked shots. Therefore, there may be some players who can count themselves unlucky that they executed the perfect shot but the defender simply got in the way. We can then use Opta’s metric of “shooting goals added” which calculates the difference between a player’s xG and xGOT. Below, you can see that Tottenham Hotspur’s Son Heung-min added the most value to his shots last season, by improving his chances of scoring by 3.8 goals from the placement of those shots. At the other end of the scale, it was Leicester City ’s Jamie Vardy with the biggest discrepancy between the chances he found himself in vs his execution of those chances, underperforming by 3.4 goals owing to poor technique in placing his on-target efforts on goal. Likewise, we can look at xGOT as a good way to measure goalkeeper performance. This provides a more accurate reflection of performance as it shows how many goals a goalkeeper is expected to have conceded based on the quality of the shots on target they have faced. We can then use this to measure the number of “goals prevented” — this compares how many goals a goalkeeper actually conceded against the number they were expected to. The higher the goals prevented number, the better the shot-stopping performance. Advertisement Last season, the best shot-stopping performance was from Hugo Lloris at Tottenham Hotspur, who kept out 5.1 goals above expectation across the season. 4. Non-penalty goals What it is: This metric requires little explanation, but it is important to consider why goalscoring tallies are often assessed by removing penalty goals from the total. Penalties themselves are not a great indicator of a player’s ability to generate chances for themselves. Of course, you can have a player who both wins and takes penalties , but often the penalty taker is handed the ball even if they were not involved in the play leading up to the foul. Changes to handball rules, and the microscopic scrutiny from the introduction of VAR also means that the number of penalties awarded was at an all-time high last season with 125 spot-kicks in total — an average of one penalty every three games. How it can be used: Penalty takers can inflate their numbers quite significantly from what is ultimately an unsustainable source of goalscoring income. Looking at last season’s top goalscorers in the Premier League, Manchester United’s Fernandes and Leicester City’s Vardy both doubled their goal tally from the spot and would be far from the top 10 goalscorers without such high-value opportunities to score (approximately 0.75 xG for those interested). Given this, it is a little more reliable to assess goalscoring opportunities in open play by looking at non-penalty goals or non-penalty xG — where you provide more of a level playing field to explore a team or player’s opportunity to score. 5. Expected assists (xA) What it is: Assists themselves can be a very poor indication of a player’s creative ability. One player could play a simple two-yard pass for their team-mate to put one in the top corner, while another could run the length of the field and put it on a plate for their team-mate to score. Hardly comparable. Also, to register an assist, the passer is reliant on the receiver to finish the chance — which does not always happen. Therefore, another extension of the expected goals framework is expected assists (xA). It works in much the same way as xG, but works back slightly in giving credit to the player who passed the ball before the shot was taken. Put simply, xA measures the expected goals value of the shot that is assisted, and is also presented as a number between zero (no chance of an assist) and one (a certain assist). How it can be used: xA can provide credit to those creative players and gives a clearer idea of how many assists a player should have, given the quality of their attacking output. We can similarly add up all of the values to explore whether a player is creating highly valuable chances or playing it a little more safe in their passing. Looking at last season, it is no surprise to see Manchester City talisman Kevin De Bruyne lead the way for the most creative player. Given that the Belgian missed a fair share of games through injury, looking on a “per 90” basis once again highlights his quality when he is in the team — providing passes worthy of an assist at a rate of more than one every three games (0.37 xA per 90). Of course, just as penalties can inflate a player’s goal output, being a set-piece taker (i.e. corners or free-kicks) can also inflate a player’s creative output, given that they have a greater opportunity to deliver the ball, unopposed, into a dangerous area with more players to attack the ball. Therefore, it is worth looking at last season’s xA among all players in open play, which shows a slightly different configuration. Here, Fernandes just about claims top spot ahead of De Bruyne, while players like Callum Hudson-Odoi and Allan Saint-Maximin show their creative quality to find team-mates in dangerous positions with their passing in open play. 6. Passes per defensive action (PPDA) What it is: Passes per defensive action (PPDA) is a proxy of pressing intensity at the team level, used to try and capture the degree to which an opponent is pressuring the opposition when they don’t have the ball. Advertisement Put simply, this metric counts how many passes a team allows the opposition to make before attempting to win the ball back with a defensive action, such as a tackle, interception, or clearance. Importantly, this metric applies only to a certain area of the pitch — the final 60 per cent of the pitch to be precise — roughly in line with the edge of the centre circle in your own half. A low PPDA number indicates higher intensity when trying to win the ball back and a higher figure indicates a team that is more passive without the ball. As you can see below, Marcelo Bielsa’s Leeds were unsurprisingly the most intense off the ball with an average PPDA of 9.3 last season, while Newcastle United were nearly half as intense in their pressing with a PPDA of 18.3 as they preferred to drop back into shape when losing possession. How it can be used: Just as above, PPDA can give an indication of a team’s intent to win the ball back. It can show which teams are more active in trying to regain possession when they lose it. Importantly, PPDA doesn’t give us any indication of the success of that strategy — it is more indicative of a team’s style in winning the ball back. As teams such as Liverpool and Manchester City have shown in recent years, pressing is most effective when the team acts in unison and knows when to pounce. Which can bring us nicely onto our next term… 7. Pressures What it is: This metric is a little more “what is says on the tin”, but it’s important to know why it is useful. Here, we turn to StatsBomb who provide this data, and define pressures as the “number of times applying pressure to the opposing player who is receiving, carrying or releasing the ball”. This can be studied at player or team level to show the intent in pressing the ball, rather than simply the outcome of making a tackle or block. The higher the number of pressures, the more the player or team attempted to engage with the opponent on the ball. Be careful here though, as more pressures may not mean a higher intensity per se, but might just mean that the team had less possession of the ball. We can account for this by adjusting the metric for the amount of possession — something we will come onto below. How it can be used: Using this information, we can consider how often that pressure was successful — i.e. the quality of the press that leads to a turnover of possession. StatsBomb pressure data via fbref provides this with “successful pressure percentage”, defined as the percentage of time that a team gained possession within five seconds of applying the pressure. As you can see below, champions Manchester City were the most co-ordinated in their press, regaining possession 32 per cent of the time when making their pressures. Meanwhile, Newcastle United remained rooted to the bottom of the table once again, alongside relegation sufferers Sheffield United with a pressure success of 25 per cent. Unfortunately, there is not a silver bullet metric for measuring pressing among teams, but using the PPDA metric alongside this pressure data can be useful to build a picture of a team’s style to win the ball back and understand how successful they are when they do look to regain possession. Advertisement 8. Possession-adjusted metrics What it is: When considering defensive metrics (e.g. tackles, blocks, interceptions), a player’s ability is not represented reliably by the raw numbers. A busy defender isn’t always a good one , and many defensive metrics most often represent a team or player’s style rather than their quality. One way we can help to overcome this issue is to adjust these defensive metrics based on the amount of possession a team has. Why do we do this? Essentially, a player can only perform a defensive action when their team does not have the ball. If a team has less possession of the ball, they have more opportunities to defend. Therefore, it is difficult to reliably compare the defensive contribution between, for example, Manchester City vs Newcastle United based on the raw frequency of defensive actions (e.g. blocks per 90 minutes). What we can do is adjust these defensive statistics for the number of times that they make these actions for every 1,000 opponent touches — which allows us to assess all players on more of a level playing field. How it can be used: Let’s run through an example. Manchester City full-back Joao Cancelo averages 2.4 interceptions per 90, which was enough to rank him 16th among all defenders in the Premier League last season. When adjusting for possession, he jumps to 4.2 interceptions per 1,000 opponent touches, which ranks him 9th among the group of defenders. This accounts for the fact that Manchester City were so dominant in possession, so gives more credit to Cancelo’s actions when City don’t have the ball. This is definitely one to look out for when you next see a players’ defensive statistics — more actions does not necessarily mean a better defender. 9. Field tilt What it is: Field tilt is a simple way of showing the territorial dominance between teams. Put simply, it measures the share of possession a team has in a game, considering only touches or passes in the attacking third. So, if Team A makes a total of 80 final-third passes, and Team B attempts just 20 final-third passes, Team A has a field tilt of 80 per cent. The better attacking teams usually dominate this metric because they have more of the ball in attacking areas. As you can see below, Manchester City and Liverpool, in particular, were suffocating teams by keeping possession in the attacking third last season. How it can be used: Field tilt is useful in revealing which side is more dominant in matches. Rather than simply looking at the average possession statistics, field tilt provides a clearer picture of where that possession is. It’s not always about simply keeping the ball, it’s about getting into the areas that matter. Likewise, it can be an interesting way to explore the change in a team’s dominance in the final third, over time. For example, in the 2019-20 season, Aston Villa had a field tilt of 41 per cent, meaning the opposition had more passes in their final third than Villa did in the opponent’s final third. It also ranked Villa as 18th in the Premier League for such territorial dominance that season. In contrast, Villa had a field tilt of 50 per cent in the 2020-21 season which was the ninth-best in the league. They were having a larger share of the play in the opposition’s final third than they did in the previous season, getting the ball into greater areas of threat for longer. In isolation, field tilt metrics may not provide too much insight towards a team’s success, but it does give an indication of their style in getting the ball into advanced areas compared with the opposition. 10. Game state What it is: Another straightforward term, but one that can provide crucial context when evaluating a team’s metrics. Game state refers to whether the team is in a losing, drawing or winning position when they are performing certain actions. This is important to consider, as it can heavily influence a team’s approach during the game. A team that is losing is more likely to chase the game by taking more shots and creating more chances. By contrast, a team that is winning might be more likely to defend a lead and subsequently create fewer chances because of the game state they find themselves in. How it can be used: As outlined above, the main use of this is to provide further context as to why a team may have certain performance metrics. For example, Tottenham Hotspur didn’t attempt a single shot in the second half at home to Arsenal last season. Instantly, this suggests weak attacking play from Spurs, but they had built a 2-0 lead before half-time. Therefore, the game state meant Spurs were in a winning position, so their low attacking output was contextualised by them protecting their lead. Looking at the game state across the season for each team, we can see that Spurs actually spent a long time in a winning position compared with others in the league, something which is likely to have fuelled the frustration towards the recently-departed Jose Mourinho, as Spurs often retreated after taking the lead. Meanwhile, many may point to champions Manchester City having the lowest goals scored in a season since Pep Guardiola arrived (83 goals), but the added context is that they spent more than half their time in the lead — more than any other team in the league — and were not obliged to score any additional goals to pick up three points. Advertisement Game state can determine the tactical approach taken by a team, and provides useful context when assessing both attacking and defensive metrics at the player or team level. 11. Sequences and possessions What it is: This could be a whole article on its own, but the principle of sequences and possessions is very simple. A sequence starts with a player making a controlled action on the ball — i.e. making a pass is controlled but making a tackle is not controlled. Opta defines a sequence as a “passage of play which belongs to one team and are ended by defensive actions, stoppages in play or a shot”. For example, if a team makes 15 passes and works it forward before the opposition defender clears it out for a throw-in, that would be one sequence. When the player throws it back in to a team-mate, that starts a second sequence but importantly, the team still has possession of the ball. Therefore, possessions are the combination of one or more sequences in a row belonging to the same team. That possession continues until the opposition wins the ball back by making a controlled action on the ball themselves — thus starting their own sequence of play. Think of it like a chain — the sequences are the individual links which join together to make the overall chain (i.e. possession). How it can be used: These metrics help us to build a wider picture of a team or player, beyond simple event metrics (i.e. a pass). It can help to show the style of a team in how many passes they tend to have within a sequence — i.e. Manchester City tend to have more passes within a sequence of play than Burnley do. By looking at the number of possessions between the teams, we can understand the style and tempo of games . Essentially, we can look at how many times the ball changed hands between the teams during the game (i.e. Team A has it until Team B has it, which continues until Team A wins it back, etc). This can help show the approach taken in games, with more possessions indicative of a higher tempo and a more frenetic game. There are many more avenues to take this information, but it shows the value of adding further context to understand what is occurring on the pitch based on individual events.
